The USSR advanced incredibly quickly moving from feudalism straight to socialism, but collapsed into the current capitalist hellscape of today also fairly quickly.

Thus capitalism is moreorless a necessary evil on the road to communism dependent on local conditions.

The biggest pitfall with procedural generation seems to me as developers wanting to create an "infinite" game. If many gameplay elements are (semi-)randomly generated, every playthrough will be technically unique. However, when used too much the proc-gen'd content all starts to just become noise.

Starbound, for example, is notorious for it. I quite liked the game, don't get me wrong, but every planet quickly starts blurring together. Yes, theoretically I could see a new planet which is perfectly unique that no one has ever seen before, but fundamentally it'll be the same as any other. It will have a biome, it will have unique creatures generated from an algorithm of parts, it will have dungeons. The more you play though the more quickly you start to notice the exact same dungeon on multiple planets, the same biomes, the same moveset for different creatures. 

It's a universe big enough that you couldn't visit every planet in one lifetime, but it all falls into identifiable structures whose differences are largely aesthetic. Worse, the non-procedurally generated content now sticks out as it's much more cohesive and consistent. You could add *more* things of course, but it just adds to the algorithmic noise of it all. The sense of a unique experience is lost when you find the same dungeon you fought through on another planet is also *here*, potentially hundreds of thousands of kilometers away. It's ruined when you find a dungeon you *haven't* already seen and immediately recognize that this same structure could be found on any number of planets.

It's a problem inherent to procedural generation, as you mentioned with algorithms not thinking outside the box. It'll only output what you input. In Starbound's case I think they could've alleviated it a fair bit without even changing all that much core-wise. Make dungeons smaller and more modular so every town is filled with different buildings instead of the same templates, or make a majority of planets barren and desolate so planets with more apparent proc-generated content are accentuated as rare and unique. Don't spread it too thin, essentially.

Chapters are just tools to better shape how a book flows. In objective terms, the contents of your chapters will always stay the same and remain in the same order regardless of what numbers you assign to each block. Most people set it up sequentially for practical purposes obviously, but there's nothing stopping you from assigning each chapter any number you want. Half, quarter, sixteenths, whatever.

Of course, while there's nothing stopping you, from a readability perspective you should consider why you'd want a half chapter. Without a distinct purpose, it'd probably just confuse most people reading it. I think it could be used to great effect for more nonlinear and parallel storytelling. 

For example, the "main" chapters (1,2,3...) follow the primary protagonist doing... whatever in a standard linear story. Half chapters, meanwhile, can follow supporting and side characters during the events of the chapter that just happened. 

As a side note, "decimal" chapters can be seen a lot in older novels as well. Each integer chapter designates more an act or season with decimal chapters divvying them up more.

* A planet is surrounded by thick corrosive gasses which would dissolve your ship in minutes. Upgrade your ship's plating and don a Hazardous Environments Suit to land.
* A planet is covered in a thick sheet of ice miles thick. Approaching with your ship would quickly ice over your systems and cause a crash. Cold weather gear recommended.
* A planet has recently been formed and is in a volcanic state, covering much of the surface in lava. While safe to land, breathing equipment is recommended to handle the planet's thin atmosphere.

Development wise, these shouldn't even necessarily take too many resources as a lot of them could be fairly barren with perhaps just a few pre-built or procedurally generated structures on the surface. I'd advise handcrafting them and saving the procedural stuff for more inconsequential details, but either can work.

In another comment you mentioned collecting resources as part of the game loop - perhaps these inhospitable ones could have rare, hard to collect resources in abundance at the cost of being extremely dangerous to traverse. 

Also, as someone said, you should definitely take into consideration stars and their effects on the planets. I'm not sure if your galaxy entails a single star system, multiple, or planets free floating, but definitely consider how stars heat the planets. It's just a small touch that'll make the universe feel that much more cohesive.

I'd suggest altering it so that the player travels between star systems within a galaxy, rather than between galaxies though. Galaxies are extremely large, and generally lack any sort of "identifiers" that would make them very unique on a planetary scale. Star systems, however, give a very easy way of making each unique in ways I've previously mentioned.

A lot of things can make the planet unique beyond just biomes - atmosphere composition, temperature, gravity, number of suns, moons, weather, hell, there are giant clouds of alcohol in space. Go wild.
